title: Field Sampling and Laboratory Analysis of Microzooplankton in Small Wetlands
author: Evhenii Hordiienko

steps.title: Record site parameters and photograph
steps.instruction: Record the exact GPS coordinates (50.991293, 34.473122), water depth (0.3–0.8 m), dominant vegetation (sedges, sphagnum, duckweed), water colour, peat layer thickness, and any visible disturbances; photograph the overall site and each micro‑biotope.

steps.title: Collect water samples from micro‑biotypes
steps.instruction: Collect 3–5 water samples, each 0.5–1 L, from distinct micro‑biotypes (open water, among duckweed/sedges, near sphagnum, bottom detritus) by gently submerging containers to capture water with surface detritus, plant fragments, and sediment; label each container immediately, transport in shade, and begin processing within 2–4 hours of collection.

substeps.instruction: Select a micro‑biotype and position the container just below the surface.
Gently submerge to collect water with associated detritus and sediment.
Label the container with site, micro‑biotype, date, and time.
Transport containers in shade.
Start laboratory processing within 2–4 hours of collection.

steps.title: Settle samples at room temperature
steps.instruction: Allow each collected sample to stand undisturbed at room temperature for 30–90 minutes; do not stir or agitate the containers after the settling period.

steps.title: Prepare microscope slides from subsamples
steps.instruction: Using a pipette, withdraw subsamples from the surface, middle, and bottom layers of each settled sample; place 1–2 drops on a microscope slide, apply a coverslip, and repeat to produce 5–10 slides per original sample for representative coverage.

substeps.instruction: Withdraw a small volume from the surface layer with a pipette.
Withdraw a small volume from the middle layer with a pipette.
Withdraw a small volume from the bottom layer with a pipette.
Place 1–2 drops of each subsample on a clean slide.
Apply a coverslip to each drop.
Prepare a total of 5–10 slides per original sample.

steps.title: Screen samples under stereomicroscope and compound microscope
steps.instruction: Examine the slides first with a stereomicroscope at 10–40× to locate larger organisms (e.g., Daphnia, insect larvae), then switch to a compound microscope at 100× for an overview and 200–400× for detailed identification; record taxa, relative abundance, and observed behavior.

substeps.instruction: Screen at 10–40× on a stereomicroscope for larger organisms.
Switch to a compound microscope at 100× for an overview of the community.
Increase magnification to 200–400× for specific taxonomic identification.
Record taxa, relative abundance, and any observed behavior.

steps.title: Identify organisms using taxonomic keys
steps.instruction: Identify observed organisms with standard identification keys (e.g., Foissner for ciliates, Koste for rotifers), giving special attention to Gastrotricha and free‑living Nematoda; document identifications with photographs and video recordings.

substeps.instruction: Consult Foissner’s key for ciliates.
Consult Koste’s key for rotifers.
Focus identification on Gastrotricha and free‑living Nematoda.
Capture representative photographs and video clips of identified taxa.

steps.title: Evaluate saprobity level
steps.instruction: Assess saprobity based on the dominance of saprophytic groups; high numbers of saprophytic ciliates (Paramecium, Vorticella, Stentor), rotifers, nematodes, or gastrotrichs indicate a β‑mesosaprobic level with α‑elements.

substeps.instruction: Determine the dominant taxonomic groups in the sample.
If saprophytic ciliates, rotifers, nematodes, or gastrotrichs are abundant, assign a saprobity classification (e.g., β‑mesosaprobic with α‑elements).

steps.title: Record data and fix subsamples
steps.instruction: Record all raw data and observations in a laboratory notebook; if preservation is required, fix subsamples with 4 % formaldehyde or Lugol’s solution; archive all digital images and field notes.

substeps.instruction: Enter raw counts, abundances, and behavioral notes into a data sheet.
If needed, add 4 % formaldehyde or Lugol’s solution to subsamples for fixation.
Save all photographs, videos, and field‑note files in a structured digital archive.
